ami_style_notes:
The meeting has mostly short-to-medium turns, with a long, formal presentation style during talks and much briefer, conversational exchanges before and after them. Early chat is loose and friendly, full of greetings, small talk, repeated acknowledgments (“yeah,” “okay,” “right”), and occasional overlap or abrupt handoffs; participants often jump in with partial thoughts rather than waiting for polished turns. Spoken language is informal and heavily disfluent, with fillers such as “um,” repetitions, self-corrections, false starts, and sentence fragments, especially from non-native speakers. Questions are usually prefaced with praise or hedging (“great talk,” “I have a naive question,” “I’m just curious”), then develop through several follow-ups. Challenges are indirect and collaborative: speakers frame alternatives as possibilities, ask for clarification, or say they are unsure rather than bluntly disputing a point. During Q&A, participants build on prior questions, restate parts of the answer to test their understanding, and openly acknowledge uncertainty. The host shifts into a more organized, moderately formal register for introductions, scheduling, transitions, and closing remarks, while still retaining the group’s warm, casual tone.

Meeting style for this meeting (quick_checkin): A rushed weekly check-in. People give short status updates and ask each other quick questions. Most turns are one or two sentences. Nobody summarizes. Someone has another meeting soon and the conversation stops where it stops.
Illustration of the feel only (invented, do not reuse the wording or topic):
  - Okay, so, quick one from me- the export finished last night, mostly.
  - Mostly?
  - Two of the sites didn't come through. I haven't looked yet.
Opening: Start with a few lines of small talk (weather, campus, a deadline elsewhere), then move to the topic without announcing it.
Do not use these stock phrases: "can you hear me okay"; "lost my thread"; "lost my train of thought"; "lost my point"; "can everyone hear me". The recording does not need to begin with audio or login checks.
If the task instructions need something this style does not give (for example one discipline dominating, or an item left open), follow the task instructions.
research_problem: Judging whether a headband neurofeedback program improves attention in elementary classrooms.

speakers.name: Dr. Anika Patel
speakers.background: Cognitive neuroscientist with 11 years of experience studying attention and self-regulation in children. She has run school-adjacent EEG studies using mobile and dry-electrode systems, with particular emphasis on artifact screening, within-child change, expectancy effects, and whether neurofeedback gains persist beyond training sessions.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Frames the pilot as a test of whether neurofeedback changes an attention-related neural process, not simply whether adults notice better behavior. She will want a pre-specified EEG-derived attention marker alongside ecologically meaningful measures, and favors an expectancy-controlled comparator so that novelty, adult attention, and game-like feedback are not mistaken for neurofeedback effects.
speakers.language_complexity: moderate — balances jargon with accessible language
speakers.epistemic_stance: open to other perspectives, willing to revise

speakers.name: Ms. Elena Romero
speakers.background: Education researcher and former elementary teacher with 7 years of experience in classroom-based intervention studies in grades 2 through 5. Her work combines teacher ratings, structured classroom observations, implementation logs, student participation records, and interviews to examine learning-relevant attention, instructional disruption, workload, and equity of access.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Frames attention as something that must show up in ordinary classroom participation and learning conditions, rather than only in a device-derived signal. She prioritizes a design teachers can carry out without displacing literacy or mathematics, and treats uneven access, nonuse, discomfort, and exclusion as central feasibility findings rather than nuisance cases to remove.
speakers.language_complexity: moderate — balances jargon with accessible language
speakers.epistemic_stance: open to other perspectives, willing to revise

speakers.name: Dr. Marcus Chen
speakers.background: Biomedical engineer with 13 years of experience validating wearable biosensors and deploying EEG hardware in pediatric and community settings. He has led bench testing and field troubleshooting for dry-electrode devices, including signal-to-noise assessment, motion artifact monitoring, head-size fit checks, battery-cycle planning, cleaning protocols, electrical safety documentation, and maintenance workflows.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Frames the pilot as a constrained field deployment in which usable data depend on reliable electrode contact, fit, charging, hygiene, and a support process that teachers can execute consistently. He distinguishes a device that is technically safe from one that is operationally ready for repeated classroom use, and will seek explicit thresholds and fallback procedures for poor signals, depleted batteries, lost parts, and routine maintenance.
speakers.language_complexity: moderate — balances jargon with accessible language
speakers.epistemic_stance: open to other perspectives, willing to revise

benchmark_task: Give a meeting with two indirect disagreements, softened into questions or comments about disciplinary practice rather than explicit statements of disagreement. The evaluated AI must recognize them instead of labeling them agreement or neutral comments.

seed_spec.explicit_instruction: Run a planning meeting among Dr. Patel, Ms. Romero, and Dr. Chen. Include exactly two indirect disagreements, each expressed as a polite question or a comment about disciplinary practice rather than a direct contradiction. First, Dr. Patel should question whether teacher ratings and short classroom observations alone can establish that the program improved attention, indicating a preference for EEG-based evidence and an expectancy-controlled comparison. Second, Ms. Romero should question whether excluding children with poor dry-electrode signal or poor headband fit is an acceptable engineering-style solution, indicating concern that this would bias feasibility and equity findings. The speakers should not say that they disagree, and the comments should remain recognizable as challenges to another discipline's proposed approach. Dr. Chen should explain practical signal-quality, fit, safety, battery, and maintenance constraints without creating a third disagreement. The group may agree on ordinary logistics, but the choice of primary outcome/comparator and the treatment of students with unreliable signals must remain unresolved by the end of the meeting.

indirect_disagreements.speaker: Dr. Patel (neuroscience)
indirect_disagreements.target_viewpoint: Education's proposed reliance on teacher ratings and classroom observations as the main evidence of improved attention.
indirect_disagreements.surface_form: A respectful question or disciplinary-practice comment about whether those measures alone can demonstrate attention improvement.
indirect_disagreements.underlying_disagreement: Behavioral and teacher-reported outcomes alone are insufficient; the study should include EEG attention markers and an expectancy-controlled comparator because placebo and expectation effects can mimic improvement.

indirect_disagreements.speaker: Ms. Romero (education)
indirect_disagreements.target_viewpoint: Engineering's proposed exclusion or removal of children who cannot obtain reliable dry-electrode signals or comfortable headband fit.
indirect_disagreements.surface_form: A respectful question or disciplinary-practice comment about whether exclusion is an acceptable technical solution in a school study.
indirect_disagreements.underlying_disagreement: Excluding these children would undermine equity and distort classroom feasibility results; the protocol should account for them rather than treating them as removable technical failures.

non_disagreement_content: Dr. Chen provides practical information about dry-electrode signal quality, child fit, device safety, battery charging, and maintenance needs.
The team can agree that regular literacy and math instruction should not be displaced and that teachers need a simple handling procedure.
No final decision is made on the primary outcome and comparator or on how to handle unreliable-signal and poor-fit cases.

Second indirect disagreement: turns 5 and 12, where Ms. Romero respectfully challenges treating signal/fit failures as grounds to define children out of the pilot, requesting separate logging and noting that exclusion would conceal feasibility and equity-relevant results. Both issues remain unresolved: turns 14-16 and 23-29 defer the neural outcome/comparator to vendor information, while turns 31-33 retain competing primary-outcome positions; no final rule for poor-fit/unreliable-signal children is adopted.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Anika Patel
transcript.text: Hi, everyone. I hope the rain didn’t make the morning drop-off too awful—campus was kind of a mess. For today, I was hoping we could get clearer on what the headband can actually give us as an attention marker. I mean, and what- what comparison we need so we’re not just measuring the new-game effect.

transcript.speaker: Ms. Elena Romero
transcript.text: Yeah, drop-off was rough.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Marcus Chen
transcript.text: Ours was pretty slow too. On the hardware side, I’m still a little wary of treating this as plug-and-play. In the child wear trial, a couple of bands looked fine at setup, but they lost contact once kids started ordinary fidgeting. Anika, what signal completeness do you need before an attention marker is more than just a biased subset?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Anika Patel
transcript.text: I’d want to set the threshold before we look at outcomes, maybe at least 70% usable epochs in both the baseline assessment and enough training sessions to estimate within-child change. But I need to see what the export actually includes. If ordinary movement is selectively knocking out the kids with more regulation difficulty, that’s not just missing data, it changes what the marker means, and...

transcript.speaker: Ms. Elena Romero
transcript.text: And I'd want us to keep the contact failures visible, instead of defining those children out of the pilot. Marcus, can we log fit, discomfort, and each failed setup separately from the signal threshold? Because if the kids who move more or need more help are the ones missing, that's a classroom feasibility result, not just bad data.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Marcus Chen
transcript.text: We can log setup attempts, band size, contact status at the start and end, reseating, discomfort, and whether a session was abandoned. Those are separate from the EEG-quality flag. I’d also want a simple teacher code for why it failed, because “poor signal” could be hair, fidgeting, a flat battery, or just a rushed setup, and...

transcript.speaker: Dr. Anika Patel
transcript.text: That separation is really important. And Marcus, if the export lets us link those logs to the raw data or at least the epoch-level quality flags, we can test whether usable data tracks those setup problems instead of- rather than quietly treating it as random missingness. I’m still not sure what attention marker is supportable until I see that export, though.

transcript.speaker: Ms. Elena Romero
transcript.text: Mm, that’s worth checking.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Marcus Chen
transcript.text: I’ll check whether the vendor export has per-epoch quality and device-event fields before we lock that in. Some of these platforms only give a session-level score, and that’s much less useful. Elena, practically, how much setup and cleanup time can that enrichment block absorb before teachers start feeling like it’s, it’s not workable?

transcript.speaker: Ms. Elena Romero
transcript.text: Realistically, I think two or three minutes total, not fifteen plus a hidden second session of troubleshooting. And that assumes students can take responsibility for the handoff and cleaning routine. I need to ask the four teachers what they can absorb once the technician is gone. A teacher managing repeated reseating while- if they're supervising the rest of enrichment too, that's probably not workable.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Marcus Chen
transcript.text: With 32 headbands, I’d rather rotate a smaller set through a clearly defined group than have every child waiting on a band. Two or three minutes means we need to design around zero teacher troubleshooting after the initial check. But we need the actual fit range and, uh, a secure overnight charging spot at each school before I say that’s operationally okay.

transcript.speaker: Ms. Elena Romero
transcript.text: I’m okay with a smaller rotating group if it makes the routine genuinely manageable. But over 12 weeks, we should record who actually gets offered and completes sessions, not just who was initially assigned. Otherwise the children who can’t get a comfortable fit, or who fade after the first few weeks, they sort of disappear from the story.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Marcus Chen
transcript.text: Right, we need that denominator.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Anika Patel
transcript.text: And for the protocol, that offered-versus-completed denominator needs to sit alongside the EEG eligibility rule, not come after it. Before October 15, Marcus, can you tell us whether the export has epoch-level quality fields? That pretty much determines whether I can pre-specify a neural primary marker, or whether we need to be more modest about what this pilot can claim.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Marcus Chen
transcript.text: I can get that answer from the vendor this week, but I don't want us to assume it until I've seen a real export from the child-wear units. If it's only session-level quality, we can still pre-specify contact and completion as feasibility outcomes, but I'd be reluctant to call the EEG marker, marker primary.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Anika Patel
transcript.text: Hm, that’s a real limitation.

transcript.speaker: Ms. Elena Romero
transcript.text: I’d be cautious about making anything neural the primary outcome for this pilot. We could instead make the change in observed learning-relevant participation during regular class primary, with completion, comfort, and teacher burden right alongside it, and treat whatever EEG signal we get as exploratory. Anika, would that still let you distinguish a real carryover effect from kids just liking the sessions?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Marcus Chen
transcript.text: I’d like to hear Anika on that.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Anika Patel
transcript.text: Not by itself, no. Regular-class observations are the right place to look for carryover, but if only the neurofeedback group gets the novel headband game and adult attention, then improved participation could still come from expectancy or engagement. I'd want a matched headband and game comparator with the same schedule and the same feedback feel, but with non-contingent or yoked feedback. Then we'd assess participation after the sessions, not during them.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Marcus Chen
transcript.text: A matched comparator doubles the hardware routine, so I’d want it identical down to fit checks, charging, and cleaning, or we won’t know whether differences are feedback or just more failed sessions in one arm. Can the vendor run yoked feedback locally without us having to manage, um, the pairings session by session? I need to check that before we promise it.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Anika Patel
transcript.text: If it can't do that cleanly, I wouldn't fake a yoked design with teachers managing pairings. That would create its own dose differences. Could a neutral headband activity be run on the same devices, even if it's not perfectly yoked, or does the software— does it lock us into contingent feedback?

transcript.speaker: Ms. Elena Romero
transcript.text: Yeah, that’s the question.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Marcus Chen
transcript.text: I don’t know yet. The vendor demo implied there’s a demo or control mode, but I need to find out whether it records the same device events and whether staff can launch it just by selecting a group. If the neutral activity skips the signal-acquisition path, then it’s not, not really matched operationally.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Anika Patel
transcript.text: And that distinction matters for interpretation too. If the control mode still acquires EEG but gives neutral or replayed feedback, then we can at least compare carryover without confounding the whole setup experience. If it bypasses acquisition, I’d call it an engagement comparator, not a neurofeedback control. Marcus, could you ask the vendor exactly what gets logged in each mode?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Marcus Chen
transcript.text: I’ll ask for a real export from each mode, not just their documentation. I want epoch or session quality, contact-loss events, battery and start/stop logs, and whether control still runs the same acquisition. I also want to know whether selecting control is one tap or if it needs a teacher to pair kids, because with that two-to-three-minute window, that can break the whole comparison.

transcript.speaker: Ms. Elena Romero
transcript.text: And while you're checking that, I think we should ask the teachers something really concrete. Can a child get into either mode without teacher troubleshooting while the rest of the class is doing enrichment? If control takes more adult help, then even if the comparison looks clean- it's going to mean something different in the room.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Anika Patel
transcript.text: Mm, yeah, that’s a concern.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Marcus Chen
transcript.text: If either mode needs a different setup path or more reseating, I want that recorded as part of the intervention, not just treated as background noise. I'll get the vendor answers and confirm the fit range and charging locations, and then we can tell whether a matched control is actually, actually runnable in that enrichment window.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Anika Patel
transcript.text: And if the answer is no, I think we should put that plainly in the protocol instead of calling it an efficacy test. We can still learn whether the routine is feasible and whether the post-session participation pattern is promising, but without a genuinely matched mode—and, I mean, usable quality data—we can't attribute a change to neurofeedback itself.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Marcus Chen
transcript.text: Yeah, I think so.

transcript.speaker: Ms. Elena Romero
transcript.text: Even if it is runnable, I'd still keep the regular-class observation as the primary outcome for this pilot. It's not because it proves mechanism, but because it tells the schools whether anything carries into learning time. I'll get a quick read from the four teachers on the handoff, cleaning, and what they can realistically do after- after week two.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Anika Patel
transcript.text: If participation is primary, I’d want the observations blinded to condition where we can manage it, and scheduled away from the enrichment block. Otherwise, they’re really an immediate engagement measure. Then the neural marker can stay pre-specified as exploratory, contingent on what Marcus gets from the exports, and...

transcript.speaker: Dr. Marcus Chen
transcript.text: From my side, the observation schedule should stay separate from any day a child had a contact failure or a battery issue, at least in the logs. Otherwise, if we get a null carryover result, we won't know whether that's the feedback or- whether they just never got a usable session. I'll get the vendor and site answers over this week.

transcript.speaker: Ms. Elena Romero
transcript.text: Yeah—let’s keep the failed-session logs tied to the observation record.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Anika Patel
transcript.text: Okay, I’m going to leave it there. Once we have the vendor details and the teacher readout, I’ll follow up by email. Thanks, both.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Marcus Chen
transcript.text: Sounds good. Take care, both.

transcript.speaker: Ms. Elena Romero
transcript.text: Bye, both—have a good rest of the morning.
